claims.text: The proposed intervention is to deposit an atomically thin tungsten carbide interlayer on tungsten surfaces before copper consolidation.
The tungsten carbide interlayer is intended to be epitaxially aligned and crystalline.
The intervention will produce an ultra-thin crystalline tungsten carbide layer at the tungsten–copper interface.
The tungsten carbide interlayer will reduce thermal boundary resistance at the tungsten–copper interface.
The tungsten carbide interlayer will minimize phonon scattering.
Tungsten carbide provides a lattice-matched bridge across the tungsten–copper interface.
Atomic-scale interlayer thickness will prevent the formation of bulky, brittle interfacial phases.
Avoiding bulky, brittle phases will preserve the composite's mechanical durability.
Atomic-scale tungsten carbide will avoid compromising irradiation performance.
The modified W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will retain mechanical strength or durability relative to the unmodified control.
The modified composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to the unmodified control.
Fusion-reactor divertor and joint materials experience high temperature, high heat flux, and intense radiation flux.
Tungsten and a copper-based heat sink are used together in fusion-divertor applications.
The conductivity and durability benefit will persist at fusion-relevant operating temperatures and neutron or ion irradiation levels.
The magnitude of conductivity improvement may vary with tungsten carbide interlayer thickness and interfacial crystallinity.
The conductivity enhancement may depend on processing conditions and interlayer uniformity.
Standard W–Cu composites have unmodified, random tungsten–copper interfacial structures.
